name: Clang
baseline: GCC (gcc and llvm-gcc; version not named on the cited 2008 page, gcc 4.2 on the 2009 follow-up page)
workload: Serially compiling every file of two programs with Clang, gcc and llvm-gcc at -O0, split by stage: Sketch (Objective-C Cocoa example, about 7,500 source lines, every file includes Cocoa/Cocoa.h) and 176.gcc (gcc-2.7.2.2 from SPECINT 2000, about 220,000 lines of C).
claimed_speedup: Sketch: 'over 90% faster on -fsyntax-only' than gcc. 176.gcc: 'Clang still comes in at ~29% faster versus gcc on -S -O0 -g and ~20% faster versus llvm-gcc'. The same page adds that LLVM optimizers are 'substantially (30-40%) faster than the GCC optimizers at a given -O level' (no data given).
compiler_and_flags: Stages timed: -Eonly, -parse-noop, -fsyntax-only, -emit-llvm -O0, -S -O0, -S -O0 -g (gcc uses -MM for the preprocessor stage); gcc version not named on the 2008-10-31 page (the next page, performance-2009-03-02.html, says gcc 4.2); Clang build flags not stated.
stars_or_usage: llvm-project 41k+ stars; default compiler on macOS, FreeBSD and Android
tradeoffs: Clang is one component of the llvm-project monorepo (about 600k commits), not a standalone repo. Aims at GCC compatibility, not identical extensions or diagnostics. Generated-code speed is roughly on par with GCC rather than faster; the claim here is about front-end and -O0 compile time.
caveats: First-party and old: the numbers are from 2008-10-31, against gcc of that era, on unstated hardware, before Clang compiled C++. The charts (timing-data PNGs) were not opened, only the prose figures above. The page itself warns that Clang's Objective-C debug info was very incomplete, so the -S -O0 -g row is unfair to GCC. Only -O0 was measured: the optimizing-compile claim (30-40%) has no data. The timing page was removed from main; it survives in the release_31 branch of the llvm-mirror/clang mirror. The current clang/www/features.html (opened in llvm-project) still says Clang is 'efficient when pitted head-to-head against GCC in batch mode' but now gives no numbers. Modern independent data was not reachable (phoronix.com and similar blocked): search snippets say 2023 Phoronix results for run time of compiled binaries are an effective tie between GCC 13 and Clang 17, so no run-time win is claimed. The listed licence NCSA is outdated; clang/LICENSE.TXT is Apache-2.0 with LLVM exceptions.
found_via: seed-record pass: https://clang.llvm.org (listed page, blocked), then raw files of llvm-project clang/www/features.html and llvm-mirror/clang release_31 www/performance*.html, found through WebSearch 'Clang vs GCC compile time benchmark'; repo facts from https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project

name: cmp
baseline: msgpack-c (msgpack C API, v1.3.0 in the shootout)
workload: Encoding (write test) and incremental parsing of randomly generated schemaless data (2367-byte small and 248571-byte large MessagePack objects) in the ludocode/schemaless-benchmarks suite, with the hash cost subtracted.
claimed_speedup: No speed win exists. The project only says 'Fast, Lightweight, Flexible, and Robust' (no numbers). The independent shootout shows CMP v14 slower than msgpack C 1.3.0 on write: 7.33 us vs 6.42 us (small) and 660.19 us vs 544.24 us (large) on the AMD Phenom II X6 1090T desktop; 89.75 us vs 69.21 us (small) and 9206.05 us vs 8142.64 us (large) on a Raspberry Pi. CMP is the smallest MessagePack build on the desktop (3232 vs 4088 bytes for write) but not on the Raspberry Pi size build (2324 vs 1528 bytes).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 5.3.0 on Arch Linux, -Wall -O3 -flto -fno-fat-lto-objects -DPIC -fPIC -DNDEBUG, each test run 7 times for 10 s, best and worst dropped
hardware: AMD Phenom II X6 1090T desktop; first-generation Raspberry Pi Model B rev2 (ARMv6)
tradeoffs: No internal buffers and no heap allocation, about 4k lines in cmp.c/cmp.h, C89, user supplies read/write/skip callbacks (no growable buffer, no tree parser). Small and portable rather than fast.
caveats: Recorded because the only numeric comparison anywhere reachable is the shootout above, and it contradicts any speed claim: CMP is slower than the named baseline on write and has no tree parser. The shootout was written by the author of MPack (a competitor; its own disclaimer says it may be biased) and tests CMP v14 with GCC 5.3.0 from 2016 (the MPack README now lists CMP v19), so current numbers may differ. The benchmark's CMP write code adds its own simple growable buffer, which the author notes is unfair for embedded comparisons. Tier D because the project's own claim has no numbers; the shootout is evidence about CMP, not for a win. Candidate for the not-faster shortcoming list.
